newsitem.title: USA: U.S. presses Japan on N. Korea aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. presses Japan on N. Korea aid.

text.p: The United States urged Japan on Thursday to provide food aid to famine-threatened North Korea and said this issue would be raised when Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto visits Washington on Friday.
"We believe there's a severe food shortage in North Korea," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said when asked about Japanese reluctance to donate.
"We believe that it is an international humanitarian imperative to meet that food shortage. And we call upon all countries to contribute," he told a news briefing.

Japan's top government spokesman said on Tuesday that Tokyo may not give food aid to North Korea because of a big drug seizure abroad a North Korean freighter and suspicions over Japanese nationals allegedly kidnapped by North Korean agents in the late 1970s and 1980s.
After some scepticism, the United States has become an advocate of more aid to ease severe food shortages in Stalinist North Korea that have been worsened by two years of flooding.
Washington pledged $25 million in response to recent U.N. World Food Programme appeals for $95.5 million in food aid for North Korea.

But while urging Japan to also provide aid, the United States on Thursday reaffirmed ts rejection of North Korean demands for large-scale food aid, a lifting of U.S. trade sanctions and diplomatic recognition as preconditions for entering into Korean peninsula peace talks.
"We will not agree to any preconditions to start these talks," Burns said.

U.S. officials for days have said that Pyongyang, during tortutous negotiations in New York last week, demanded large-scale food aid, diplomatic recognition and a lifting of U.S. sanctions in connection with proposed four-party peace talks.

But for the first time since South Korea's negotiators returned home from New York on Monday after Pyongyang failed to give a clear-cut answer to the U.S.-South Korea peace talks proposal, North Korea on Thursday publicly signalled those conditions itself.
The conditions were hinted at by Pyongyang's top negotiator on the peace talks issue, Kim Gye-gwan, vice minister of foreign affairs, in comments carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).

But Burns told reporters: "the essential point is this: If there's a critical food shortage in North Korea, why in the world would we link food assistance to the slow-as- molasses political talks that have taken 44 years not to begin?"

"The North Koreans have a direct interest in getting the food aid there. They surely can't want to tie it to political talks that may or may not begin anytime during this year. That's our answer," he said.

The four-way peace talks were proposed last year by Seoul and Washington and would include China as well as North Korea. The aim is to finally close the books on the 1950-53 KOrean War by replacing a frayed armistice with a permament peace treaty.
